column2: Inside a giant 1980s Manhattan record store at night, looking straight down the long main aisle: endless wooden record bins full of vinyl LP sleeves in bright colours, hand lettered genre dividers, listening booths with headphones on hooks, a high ceiling with hanging neon tubes in pink and blue, posters of eye flowers on every column, a cashier counter far away at the end, shoppers flipping through crates.

The front of two attached five storey brick tenements at 96 and 98 St. Marks Place in the East Village, New York, 1975, seen straight on from across the street: identical windows in a grid, fire escapes, stone stoops, a basement clothing shop under the stoop, people leaning out of several windows each doing something different (watering plants, a cat, a bather, someone painting), a yellow cab passing, late afternoon sun.

The corner of Ludlow Street and Rivington Street on the Lower East Side, New York, 1989, a bright summer day, looking straight down Ludlow Street: a small clothing boutique storefront on the corner with a striped awning and racks of shirts outside, old tenements with fire escapes, a hydrant, hand painted shop signs, bodega fruit stands, people on the sidewalk, a wide panoramic feeling.

Inside a 1960s Midtown Manhattan art studio loft whose walls, columns, pipes and ceiling are completely covered in crumpled silver aluminium foil and silver paint: silver helium pillow balloons floating in the air, a worn red couch in the middle, silkscreen frames leaning on the walls, a 16mm camera on a tripod, a party of artists and musicians dressed in black with sunglasses, strong bare bulb light making the silver glitter.

Inside a cramped legendary 1977 Bowery punk club, New York, looking straight at the small low stage at the far end: walls and ceiling layered with years of stickers, flyers and graffiti, a long bar on the right with neon beer signs that say only N3W, a low stage with amplifiers, a drum kit and a band in leather jackets playing, a packed crowd in leather and torn shirts in front, a red and blue stage glow, smoke.

The community room of a Bronx apartment building in August 1973, a summer back to school party at night: low ceiling, cinder block walls, a DJ table at the far end with two turntables, a mixer and huge speaker cabinets, the DJ with one hand on a record, young people dancing in the middle of the floor, a breakdancer spinning, folding chairs along the walls, coloured lights, a hand drawn party flyer on the wall that says COUNTED.

A sunny summer morning in 1958 on East 126th Street in Harlem, New York, looking straight across the street at a row of brownstones: about fifty jazz musicians in suits, hats and overcoats gathered on the stoop, the steps and the sidewalk of one brownstone, posing for a group photograph, a dozen children sitting along the curb in front, ornate iron railings, brownstone cornices, trees.

Inside a small famous wedge shaped basement jazz club in Greenwich Village, New York, looking from the wide back of the room toward the narrow point of the triangle where a tiny bandstand sits about twelve metres away: red walls hung with framed black and white photographs of musicians, low ceiling, small round tables with candles receding toward the band, a piano trio playing upright bass, piano and drums on the bandstand, warm amber light. The nearest tables and the foreground floor are empty, every guest sits at the far tables.

Inside a grand historic Harlem theatre on amateur night, 1950s, standing on the stage looking out at the audience: a packed red and gold auditorium with two curved balconies, ornate boxes, red velvet seats, a spotlight beam from the back, the whole audience cheering and pointing, a big tree stump on a pedestal at the side of the stage, gold proscenium arch around the view.

The lobby of a famous old bohemian hotel on West 23rd Street, New York, 1960s: a grand wrought iron staircase spiralling up, the walls crowded to the ceiling with paintings and sculptures left by artists who paid their rent in art, a fireplace, a front desk with a bored clerk, a few eccentric guests, a guitar case, warm lamps, worn tile floor.

Jones Street in Greenwich Village, New York, a cold grey winter afternoon in 1963, looking down the long narrow street toward West 4th Street: slushy snow on the empty asphalt in the foreground, parked early 1960s cars along both curbs, five storey brick walk-up tenements with fire escapes on both sides, bare trees, and far down the middle of the street, about fifteen metres away, a young couple walking toward the camera arm in arm, he in a brown suede jacket and jeans, she in a green coat. The foreground and the near half of the street are empty of people.
